items.title: Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom
items.summary: Biotech stocks are rallying as clinical wins, M&A and new drug technologies revive the sector. Here are the ETFs and stocks analysts favor.
items.body: Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains. The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive). Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI. "We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF .

items.title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
items.summary: Do British pensioners have it better or worse than those in other countries?
items.body: Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic. The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011. But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade. Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people. And funding the triple lock has already cost the state billions more than initially envisaged.

items.title: Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growth
items.summary: Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’ Andy Burnham has promised that local leaders in England will no longer have to come “cap in hand to Westminster” ahead of a fresh drive to devolve…
items.body: Andy Burnham has promised that local leaders in England will no longer have to come “cap in hand to Westminster” ahead of a fresh drive to devolve spending power in next week’s budget. In his statement on Wednesday, the chancellor, John Healey , will include plans for a new £1.5bn borrowing facility, to be drawn up in collaboration with mayors over the next two years. Regional mayors have long complained that they are constrained by their limited borrowing power – in contrast to local authorities in the US and some European countries, which commonly issue their own bonds. The borrowing plan will form part of a big devolution package aimed at boosting regional economic growth. This will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.

items.title: Piero Cipollone: Interview with Milano Finanza
items.body: Mr Cipollone, you have just attended a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Italian Banking Association. Was the digital euro one of the topics discussed? We mainly talked about tokenisation. On the subject of the digital euro, I provided an update on the status of the debates on the legislation in Brussels and on the progress of our internal preparations within the Eurosystem. Since you joined the ECB, payments have become one of the main focus areas of your work. Why are they so important for Europe’s future? Because payments constitute a strategic infrastructure for Europe and, as a central bank, ensuring the smooth functioning of payment systems falls within our mandate. Whenever we buy something online or pay for a coffee, we think about the price of what we’re buying. But we hardly ever think about how the payment is made.

items.title: Credit card defaults surge across China as older borrowers struggle to repay debt
items.summary: China is facing a surge in credit card delinquencies from a seemingly unlikely source: middle-aged borrowers who otherwise look like model citizens, with university educations and secure public-sector jobs. Chinese banks once rushed to lend to this group, confident they would…
items.body: China is facing a surge in credit card delinquencies from a seemingly unlikely source: middle-aged borrowers who otherwise look like model citizens, with university educations and secure public-sector jobs. Chinese banks once rushed to lend to this group, confident they would easily be able to pay their bills. But defaults are now rising so quickly amid an economic slowdown that lenders are ramping up efforts to dispose of their non-performing loan portfolios. The past quarter saw a roughly 50 per cent jump in the value of non-performing loans registered on the Banking Credit Assets Registration and Circulation Centre – China’s official platform where banks and consumer finance firms list and trade non-performing debt portfolios. The value of newly registered bad-loan portfolios reached 148.1 billion yuan (US$22.2 billion) in the third quarter of 2026, including principal and interest.

items.title: After SpaceX restores high-speed service, Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink agreement
items.summary: Ukraine says restrictions on Starlink and Starshield have been lifted, restoring connectivity to fast-moving military systems after disruptions.
items.body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Saturday said the company restricted Ukraine's access to its high-speed technology because Kyiv violated Starlink's terms of service. In a post on X , Musk said: "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week." He added: "SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR." Ukraine officials said earlier in the day that SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems had restored high-speed service, a day after they said the service remained throttled. Ukrainian official said the service disruption left the country vulnerable to Russian attacks. "The monitoring systems of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine officially record the restoration of the speed of Starlink/Starshield," it said in a statement .

items.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
items.summary: The chancellor will unveil AI spending aimed at shoring up the UK's defences in Wednesday's Budget.
items.body: The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats. As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit £100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms. The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats. "AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said. "I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

items.title: Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocated
items.summary: Data released under freedom of information laws reveals hundreds of projects unfinished despite Tory promises on regional equality • Can a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres? Most levelling up projects are not finished, years after funds were allocated,…
items.body: Most levelling up projects are not finished, years after funds were allocated, highlighting how ambitious Conservative promises of quick progress on regional equality have faltered. Data released under freedom of information laws and manually reviewed by the Guardian found 821 levelling up projects out of 1,347 were yet to be finalised as of May this year. Across the UK, 73 council areas that had a bid for a project accepted were yet to see a single one fully completed. The Guardian has identified 59 projects that were completed since the data was collected. Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have seen slower delivery in their levelling up projects, despite having fewer overall. North-west England and Yorkshire also had low project completion rates, but they were also the two regions allocated the most projects to begin with.

items.title: ‘Not a G2 world’: Apec chief on how the forum has changed through the years
items.summary: China is becoming more confident and ambitious, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) executive director said, as the forum returns to the country for the third time in a quarter-century. Eduardo Pedrosa, the executive director of the Apec Secretariat, told the SCMP on…
items.body: China is becoming more confident and ambitious, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) executive director said, as the forum returns to the country for the third time in a quarter-century. Eduardo Pedrosa, the executive director of the Apec Secretariat, told the SCMP on Thursday that the forum would crucially bring together people and businesses from across the globe, though he noted that the limelight on meetings between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. “There seems to be momentum building up,” he said. “Compared to last year, when the two presidents only met once at Apec, this year they will have met four times. That gives them a personal dynamic; they get to understand each other in a better, more personal way. “I hope we’ll see some stability and a better understanding of the approaches [that each country] would take,” he added.

items.title: What next for France as riots rattle markets? Three questions facing investors ahead of more protests
items.summary: French unrest pushed bond yields to a 24-year high as investors weigh budget, growth and sectors risks ahead of more protests.
items.body: France's unrest is fueling investor concerns over the country's fiscal outlook, after borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2002 earlier this week. With further demonstrations planned, fund managers are assessing whether prolonged disruption could weaken growth, undermine confidence and make it harder for the government to deliver planned budget savings. Rating agency Moody's on Friday kept its Aa3 credit rating on France, a level it still deems " high grade ," but maintained its negative outlook on the nation. "The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report. Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow its budget deficit.

items.title: Is London really the most-taxed city? Banks accused of cherrypicking data
items.summary: Lobby group’s figures, shared with John Healey, are misleading as they do not include major rival Paris, say campaigners A banking lobby group has been accused of cherrypicking data and trying to mislead the British government by claiming a tax rise for banks at next week’s…
items.body: A banking lobby group has been accused of cherrypicking data and trying to mislead the British government by claiming a tax rise for banks at next week’s budget would leave London less competitive than rival financial hubs. UK Finance, which represents banks including Lloyds, JP Morgan and Revolut, commissions an annual report tallying up all the taxes shouldered by a large bank, including corporation tax, social security, VAT and bank-specific levies. The report, put together by PwC, lists London as the most tax-intensive city, charging a “total tax rate” of 46.2%, compared with 42.2% in Amsterdam, 39.1% in Frankfurt, 29% in Dublin and 27.9% in New York. The figures have been heavily pushed by UK Finance, including in a recent letter to John Healey , the chancellor, in which it warned that banks could shift business and jobs to rival hubs if threatened with higher bills.

items.title: Why popular airplanes are getting scrapped years early
items.summary: Airplanes are getting dismantled for parts years ahead of schedule because engines and other components are in short supply.
items.body: GOODYEAR, Ariz. — An Airbus A320neo, one of the world's most popular planes, rolled off the Mobile, Alabama, factory line in July 2022, painted bright yellow for its next destination: Spirit Airlines. It was built to fly for decades. But this May, less than four years later, it was stripped for parts worth millions and crushed, the steel teeth of an excavator tearing through its fuselage at a facility on the outskirts of Phoenix. More aircraft are getting dismantled years, if not decades, earlier than expected, industry executives told CNBC. It is the result of a shortage of parts, none more precious and expensive than aircraft engines, that has exasperated airlines and driven up costs for years . Even after the engines are removed, firms are looking for parts as varied as landing gear and antennae to sell.

items.title: Rising demand from families needing Christmas help
items.summary: Charlotte Riley says more families are reaching out for help for a variety of reasons.
items.body: The number of families asking for help to afford Christmas presents is rising, according to the organiser of a charitable cause. For the past two years Charlotte Riley has collected and distributed donated gifts voluntarily as part of Christmas Kindness Appeal Jersey which she organises through Facebook. The gifts are given to families for children aged up to 18. Riley said: "What we are seeing is that each year we're getting more and more numbers coming through." She said the donated gifts helped to "take the pressure off" families in need of support. Riley said when she first started the appeal in 2024 she "didn't expect the response from the community". She said the reasons people might reach out to the appeal included unemployment, ill health and the general high cost of living. Along with more demand, Riley said there were also increasing numbers of people offering to help.

items.title: Can curry nights and canny advisers help Healey deliver a budget for everyday people?
items.summary: The chancellor has promised ‘breathing space’ for households and small businesses but global events cannot be ignored You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books Every Sunday night, the chancellor, John Healey, slips next door to Andy…
items.body: Every Sunday night, the chancellor, John Healey, slips next door to Andy Burnham’s Downing Street flat where they order a curry and chew over politics on the prime minister’s sofa. An Indian takeaway is one of the totemic issues in British politics, a “treat” fewer people can afford, like a pint at the football or soft play for the kids. Healey has promised to give Britain’s battered consumers “breathing space” in next week’s budget, but three months after taking on the job, the new chancellor also hopes to buy himself time. Key decisions will be postponed until a spending review at some point next year – including when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence: the issue that prompted Healey’s resignation as defence secretary in June, hastening Keir Starmer’s departure.

items.title: Moody's holds steady on France's credit rating as country grapples with turmoil and higher yields
items.summary: Moody's left its credit rating on France at Aa3, giving the country some relief in a week of unrest.
items.body: Moody's opted to maintain its credit rating on France as the country contended with a week of civil unrest and rising political risk. The agency kept France's credit rating at Aa3, a level Moody's still deems " high grade ," but it also maintained its negative outlook on the nation. "The negative outlook reflects the increased risk that the fragmentation of France's political landscape will continue to impair the functioning of the country's legislative institutions," Moody's said in its report. Moody's noted that it could return France's outlook to stable if its institutions can narrow the deficit. Investors were anticipating Moody's rating decision as France, the second-largest economy in the euro zone, grappled with protests and a sharp surge in bond yields.

items.title: Charity expects demand for Christmas present campaign
items.summary: The campaign, run by Little Stars, is running from today until 4 December.
items.body: A Shropshire charity has said it expects demand to be high this year for its campaign which provides Christmas presents to struggling families. Little Stars, which gives away free essentials to families in need, has launched Santa's Little Stars, which runs from Saturday 24 October to Friday 4 December. The public is asked to donate new, unwrapped toys and gifts to donation points in Shrewsbury's Darwin shopping centre. Donations are wrapped and given to children from birth to age 17, as well as pregnant women who are referred to the charity. Little Stars said 2025 was its biggest campaign year to date, and it expected demand to continue to be high due to many families continuing to face financial pressures. The charity launched Santa's Little Stars in 2020 and has given out more than 8,000 presents in that time, supporting more than 2,100 children.

items.title: ‘Cuts mean jobs’: Skydance staff brace for shake-up after $110bn megamerger
items.summary: Battle far from over after Paramount and Warner Bros deal creates new global entertainment powerhouse “It feels like the calm before the storm,” says an executive at Skydance, the newly minted media empire formed from the megamerger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery (WBD).…
items.body: “I t feels like the calm before the storm,” says an executive at Skydance, the newly minted media empire formed from the megamerger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery (WBD). “David has got what he wanted, but now there is a price to pay.” Earlier this month, David Ellison, Skydance’s chief executive, sealed the $110bn (£82bn) deal , creating a global powerhouse spanning two Hollywood studios each more than a century old, the TV networks HBO, MTV and Discovery, and news outlets CBS and CNN. Having seen off a rival bid from Netflix and faced significant political and industry opposition, in a process Ellison told employees was at times “downright ugly”, the battle is far from over for Hollywood’s newest magnate.

items.title: Retail investors are not more sophisticated than 30 years ago, says former hedge fund manager
items.summary: Retail investors trying to beat the market by buying individual stocks and complex exchange-traded funds may be better off with broad market index funds.
items.body: Retail investors who are trying to beat the market by buying individual stocks and complex exchange-traded funds may be better off with broad market index funds, according to Elm Wealth's Victor Haghani. "I'm not sure that investors are that much more sophisticated than they were 30 years ago," the firm's founder and chief investment officer told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "We still are human beings and we're subject to certain kinds of biases — particularly extrapolation bias where whatever has happened recently in the past we tend to believe that it's going to continue into the future." Haghani, who was a founding partner at hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management, emphasizes cost-effective investment strategies as a priority at his current firm. "It's an environment that continues to be tough for individual non-professionals to generate alpha," he said.

items.title: More than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027
items.summary: Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’ Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing.…
items.body: Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing. So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian. TG Jones was bought and renamed by Modella last year. Before the private equity group’s restructure won approval from creditors in July , the chain operated 180 post offices and it had been feared that as many as 60 could be closed under the shake-up. Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by Modella are expected to shut, about 65 of which have already closed and at least another 46 are to cease operating early next year. This total of 110 announced closures include the 70 containing post offices.

items.title: American embassies tighten security as Iran threat warnings intensify ahead of U.S. midterm elections
items.summary: A memo from DNI director Jay Clayton said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans.
items.body: U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday. A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well. The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu.

items.title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longer
items.summary: With storms hitting parts of the UK and the clocks going back, here are some practical ways to cope with falling temperatures.
items.body: As the UK braces for a chilly weekend, with powerful winds and heavy rain hitting parts of the country, people are looking for ways to bring some warmth to their homes without cranking up the heating just yet. It is autumn after all. But with rising energy prices making heating homes more expensive, taking action now could pay off in the long run. Experts warn, though, that if you're elderly or vulnerable you shouldn't compromise your health. To help you prepare for the chillier months, BBC News asked families and experts to share their tips for keeping your home warm and cost-effective. When it gets cold, many people turn to hot water bottles and blankets - but there are other ways to warm your body. The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers, rather than one thick layer, to trap the heat in.

items.title: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle
items.summary: The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and…
items.body: D ale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales . There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels. The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labour politicians as a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”.

items.title: What a day in customer service looks like — as AI changes everything
items.summary: Customer service can be a "really, really difficult job." Will AI make it easier — or cause even more headaches?
items.body: For Kaylee Harris, who works in customer service for a credit card company, a day at work now looks very different. Her hours used to be filled with calls, note-taking and lengthy card disclosures. Now, thanks to artificial intelligence , she can focus more on each customer, Harris told CNBC. For Shannon, AI has also changed things — but not in a good way. She works in customer service for a telecommunications company in Cardiff, Wales, and did not want to share her surname for fear of being identified by her employer. She told CNBC that AI-generated notes at her current workplace are often riddled with errors, "so I just write my own." At her previous employer, a property services company, senior management told staff to "ChatGPT it" if they didn't know the answer.

items.body: Sam Fender has responded to criticism by fans about ticket prices for his 2027 stadium tour by promising he would lower the cost, telling followers on Instagram: “They’re getting changed.” The 32-year-old musician announced his Proper Massive stadium tour earlier this week. Gavin Davis, an Instagram user, shared details of standing tickets for Fender’s show at Wembley, which were split into “front standing”, costing £130.75, and “standing”, priced at £98.85. Prices for seating ranged between £64.75 and £130.75. He said: “It got inflated well more than I’d had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on.” In his reply, Fender also criticised the division of standing tickets into front and back tiers as “bollocks”, saying this “won’t be happening” on his tour.

items.title: AI's 'Black October': Critical PHP flaws set off global security scramble
items.summary: Governments and businesses around the globe are scrambling to contain the fallout after the PHP vulnerabilities leaked online.
items.body: Cybersecurity teams around the globe are rushing to patch PHP programming language flaws this week, in an artificial intelligence safety moment that's being described as "Black October." "In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year," John Milinovich, senior director of product management at Figma, wrote in a post on X on Thursday. "Every sector from government to education to big tech and banks is being massively affected, and people are starting to freak out." Researchers at Google's Wiz and the AI firm Calif discovered major vulnerabilities in PHP in August by using advanced AI models from OpenAI and Google. But by Tuesday, the warnings had spread online, prompting governments and businesses around the globe to scramble to contain the fallout .

items.body: W hat are you stockpiling? Wes Streeting says we need water and food to last 72 hours in case of national emergency, as well as wind-up radios so that we can check in on how the apocalypse is developing in Ambridge. Personally, I have a two-week supply of jokes about the government that I can draw upon even as the zombies break down my front door. Andy Burnham, far from stockpiling, is busy chucking stuff out. This week Labour’s much cherished commitment not to allow new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea went into the skip round the back of Downing Street, where it lies next to a complete set of European Union red lines, a plan for digital ID and a signed photograph of Peter Mandelson. Tory frontbenchers waved their hands in amazement as the prime minister explained that the government is now in favour of dashing for gas.

items.title: Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan | Emily Bratt
items.summary: Working in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for others There are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “ Loudcasting ” –…
items.body: T here are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “ Loudcasting ” – playing audio, watching videos or talking on speakerphone in public spaces – is a form of antisocial behaviour that drives eight in 10 of people in the UK crazy, and I’m glad Andy Burnham is one of those eight. But while I welcome his policy to fine “headphone dodgers”, I’m not convinced it will solve the problem. This behaviour isn’t only a nuisance, but a grave indicator of a deeper societal issue: the erosion of empathy. You can’t legislate civic pride into an individualistic culture where feelings of social disconnection are widespread. From 2019 to 2021 I lived in Japan, where keeping the peace is paramount and you can be reprimanded just for talking on the bus.

The government launched a campaign on Thursday advising people to set aside three days’ worth of stores to deal with a whole range of eventualities, and some are already well under way. “I’m adding a few extra tinned foods and dried foods to each weekly shop to build up a stockpile over time,” said Lawrence Barratt, from Hythe in Hampshire. “Tinned beans, soups, chilli con carne. items.title: Corruption is voters' top issue ahead of midterm election, CNBC survey shows
items.summary: Democrats have worked to contrast economic hardship with President Trump's surging net worth and his family's lucrative business dealings.
items.body: Voters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey before the Nov. 3 midterm election. The finding follows a monthslong messaging effort by Democrats to link widespread economic dissatisfaction with what they allege is rampant corruption by President Donald Trump and his Republican allies. CNBC's survey of 1,000 registered U.S. voters found 36% of respondents pointing to government corruption as one of the most important issues facing the country right now. The cost of food and groceries came second with 34%, followed by protecting democracy and the price of gas, which garnered 23% each. The nationwide poll, which gauged attitudes about the economy, Trump, Congress, artificial intelligence, the Iran war and more, was conducted Oct. 14-18.

items.title: ‘Comfort in a bowl’: porridge hotter than ever as fibremaxxers get their oats
items.summary: Humble breakfast staple at heart of trend stirred up by health concerns and hearty spoonfuls of nostalgia The clocks may be going back in the UK this weekend, but the biggest sign winter is coming is a steaming bowl of porridge on a breakfast table. A staple for centuries,…
items.body: The clocks may be going back in the UK this weekend, but the biggest sign winter is coming is a steaming bowl of porridge on a breakfast table. A staple for centuries, porridge is traditionally made with oats, water and a pinch of salt or sugar. However, the humble dish is now experiencing its own renaissance, with the latest iterations transforming it from drab to decadent. The trend is being driven by a growing fibre-centric movement as well as by nostalgia. On social media, recipe creators are experimenting with everything from miso versions to sour cherry and pistachio butter toppings. At 26 Grains , a central London restaurant that specialises in porridge, this month’s offering includes a five-grain porridge topped with fig and red grape jam and a dollop of whipped cream. Over at Oatis in west London, toppings range from caramelised banana and tahini to mushrooms and pesto.

items.summary: Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the…
items.body: Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress. Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed. She added that many of the state’s farmers rely on specialized equipment and materials from across the border that are “unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense”.

items.title: Can a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres?
items.summary: Turning boarded-up shops into community spaces is a bigger and more complex task than just adding funding Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocated “It is nice to see something happening for once,” says Jack Vincent, a Grimsby resident, as he…
items.body: “It is nice to see something happening for once,” says Jack Vincent, a Grimsby resident, as he considers a wave of change finally arriving in a town that had become a byword for deprivation. In June, King Charles visited the Lincolnshire coastal town, celebrating the opening of a youth centre in a previously derelict Victorian warehouse building and a Care charity community drop-in centre in a vacant bank on the high street. Scaffolding also shrouds one end of the town’s shopping centre, part of which is being converted to house leisure facilities including a cinema and a food market. “It is getting better and we have got the new cinema coming,” says Vincent, who is in town with his partner and two young children.

items.title: He wants to clean up the city and banish high prices. But who is ‘London’s Batman’?
items.summary: The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-priced Freddo bars In the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets of London to tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering.…
items.body: In the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets of London to tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering. “When I said I wanted to save London, I meant it. I will not stop until every single bit of trash is off the streets,” he says in a viral video, narrated in his trademark deep, husky and (suspiciously) American voice, joined by a gang of hooded helpers clearing rubbish-strewn streets in Tower Hamlets. This was Batman’s first good deed for the capital and, in the month since relocating from Gotham, he has carried out many more: paying parking fines for those visiting loved ones in hospital, giving out “free fuel” to motorists and bringing back £1 chicken and chips to those who once savoured this cheap and filling after-school meal.

items.body: The Department of Justice filed an extraordinary lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the winner of its upcoming U.S. Senate election if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses the contest. The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the Nov. 3 election , cites what it argues is likely voter confusion from the name of another candidate appearing on the ballot, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan. The DOJ says that could help Democratic nominee Mary Peltola defeat the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, in what is expected to be a close contest. The Alaska race is among several closely watched Senate races that could determine control of the chamber. Republicans currently hold a narrow majority. The suit asks a federal judge in Alaska to bar the state from certifying "any result that may be impacted by voter confusion ...

items.title: Five key tax talking points before next week’s budget
items.summary: As the chancellor prepares for 28 October, we unpack the facts and figures – and the implications any changes could mean for you As John Healey prepares his first budget as chancellor, tax is the small word that is likely to cast a large shadow over next week’s big fiscal…
items.body: As John Healey prepares his first budget as chancellor, tax is the small word that is likely to cast a large shadow over next week’s big fiscal announcement. In its election manifesto , Labour promised not to increase the “big three”: income tax, national insurance and VAT. As a result, much of the pre-budget speculation has centred on which other levies Healey might seek to change. No one seems to like paying tax, but some taxes – or the rules around them – are more unpopular than others. Here, we look at some that have been under the spotlight recently, and the facts and figures behind them. In a recent sales pitch to voters, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch pledged to “abolish inheritance tax [IHT] as soon as we can afford it”. She said IHT was “supposed to be a tax on the super-wealthy” but had become a “tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country”.
